scientificSummary.scope: Selected MPO-/PR3-ANCA, neutrophil/complement and renal/pulmonary injury mechanisms for GPA/MPA-spectrum AAV, with a separate EGPA eosinophilic context. Abstract-level primary reports only; excludes drug-induced disease, comprehensive organ/diagnostic coverage and treatment efficacy. ANCA-negative EGPA is included, not generalized to ANCA-negative GPA/MPA.

paragraphs.text: Within the selected GPA/MPA-spectrum evidence, patient MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA IgG activated human neutrophils in vitro, while TNF priming enhanced oxidative burst and degranulation. Activated-neutrophil supernatants activated serum complement and generated C5a; C5a then primed neutrophils for further ANCA responses. Together, these experiments support a context-bound amplification model, not proof of one universal disease circuit. Alternative-complement involvement is strengthened by protection of factor-B- and C5-deficient mice from anti-MPO renal disease. Purified anti-MPO IgG caused necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis in mice; pulmonary capillaritis was reported in the separate anti-MPO splenocyte-transfer experiment, not demonstrated here for antibody alone. ANCA-stimulated neutrophils also released NETs containing MPO and PR3, and NETs were observed in inflamed human kidneys. However, tissue presence does not prove disease initiation, and serum NET measurements in one human cohort did not reliably distinguish active disease from remission or correlate with BVAS and renal indices.

EGPA is represented separately rather than treated as an interchangeable ANCA-driven extension of that model. Its genetic study linked a tendency to eosinophilia with susceptibility and distinguished MPO-ANCA-positive from ANCA-negative subgroups. In selected EGPA tissue, lytic eosinophils and eosinophil extracellular traps were present in small-vessel thrombi; EETs supported platelet adhesion in vitro, but these findings do not establish the initiating cause of clinical thrombosis. In a small cohort, circulating cell-free DNA tracked activity only in the EGPA subgroup and was not shown to derive exclusively from EETs. Serum from patients in EGPA remission induced NET formation in healthy-donor neutrophils: the overall ANCA-positive/negative comparison was not significant, despite subgroup differences reported in the source. Eosinophil count correlated with NET formation without identifying the responsible serum factor. These culture, genetic and observational findings remain distinct from mouse experiments. Full methods, cohort independence, causal generality and contemporary literature completeness have not been established by this abstract-level curation. Therapy efficacy is outside this map; provisional automatic appraisals are uncalibrated, and independent domain and external summary review remain pending.

after.text: In two retrospective AAV-GN cohorts totaling 369 patients, tissue complement-related expression was associated with renal severity and outcomes but weakly concordant with serum or deposition markers. These human associations do not establish biochemical complement activation or prove the causal renal pathway represented by the mouse experiments.
limitations: Complement transcript abundance is not a direct measurement of biochemical complement activity. No functional assays or complement-fragment measurements were performed.
Available-case subsets and incomplete modalities permit selection bias; survival models were exploratory, without competing-risk regression or multiplicity correction across all survival contrasts.
Cohort association does not establish causation, predict response to a complement inhibitor or demonstrate treatment efficacy.
Expression scores were not meaningfully correlated with BVAS; serum C4 was not associated with outcomes after adjustment.
